name: Maya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. Tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Maya, 27, and I run the claims desk at Fernhill Pet Cover, a small pet insurer with about forty staff in a seaside town. I've got a biology degree, which is handy for reading vet invoices. I live with my partner Robin, who drives buses part-time, in a flat with a damp bathroom we can't afford to leave. We've got about two weeks of money saved, because I'm still paying off a credit card from the move.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with the overnight vet invoices: a dog that ate a sock, a cat with a kidney problem, that sort of thing. I use AI tools every day, and I built a set of prompts that draft our letters and flag invoices that don't match the policy. Then I check what the tools flagged and handle the angry calls, usually from someone whose dog has died and whose claim was refused. I love the puzzle of it, and I hate that we're understaffed every single week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like these tools. I'd tell people online that AI was oversold, but that the small wins are still real, like my letter prompts. At work I'd say we should stop waiting for magic and hire two more people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's safe in that world, because the tools only do the boring bits. The thing is, Fernhill is small and keeps losing customers to the big insurers, and the pay is low. We're two weeks from trouble whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and teach the rest of the team my prompts, so we save a few hours a week. I'd pay off the last of the credit card by spring. I'd also start asking around about joining a union, because nobody at Fernhill has one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, a bit relieved. The money stress is the same as always. Honestly, I'd miss the excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Fernhill keeps losing customers. How worried are you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly worried. We lost a big contract with a vet chain last year, and the owners froze pay. If Fernhill folded, there's nothing else like it within fifty miles of the seaside here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Robin think about your work and AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robin thinks I'm a bit obsessed, which is fair. My partner Robin says the bus company has talked about self-driving buses for ten years and nothing's happened. In this picture, Robin would be right, and I'd have to hear about it.

say: I'd admit I'm **disappointed**, because the small AI wins in my work are real.
I'd tell Fernhill to stop waiting for magic and **hire two people**.
think: My **job is safe** when AI only does the boring bits.
Fernhill is **losing customers** and pay is low, so we're two weeks from trouble anyway.
do: **Teach the team** my letter prompts to save a few hours a week.
Ask around about **joining a union**, since Fernhill has none.
feel: **Flat** and **relieved** at once, missing the excitement of the tools.
S0.quote: Fernhill (the pet insurer I work for) is small and keeps losing customers to the big insurers, and the pay is low.
fieldNote: She is the rare person who'd be **disappointed** by a plateau.
Her real risk is the **firm's health**, not AI, and there's nothing similar locally.
She mixes **enthusiasm for tools** with a progressive push to unionise.

steps.text: Teach the claims team her AI letter-drafting prompts
Pay off the last of the credit card by spring
Ask a finance workers' union about joining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when workers need a say, because the tools are good and the savings are real. I'd post about how my prompts saved hours, and ask where those hours went: more pay, or fewer staff? At work I'd ask the owners to put it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm the person who'd be building the thing that shrinks my team. Checking vet invoices against a policy is pure thinking work, and the tools already do half of it. I'd probably keep a job, as the one who runs the system, but the four people under me might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fernhill to make me claims systems lead, with a pay rise, and I'd write down how the tools work so it's not all in my head. I'd do a short online course in data and automation in the evenings, the cheap one. And I'd organise the team into the union so the cuts at least come with proper terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. I like this stuff, and I can see it costs my friends their jobs. That bit sits badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, mostly, who's twenty and lives with his gran. He's slow with the tools and quick with people. If they cut, he goes first, and I'd be the one whose prompts did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd build the system and also organise against the cuts. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think those go together, because whoever builds it knows what it can't do. I'd use that to argue for keeping people on the hard calls, the dead pets and the complaints. Building the tool and fighting for my team are the same job to me.

say: I'd ask where the **saved hours** go: more pay or fewer staff?
I'd ask Fernhill's owners to put **job promises** in writing.
think: I'm the one **building the thing** that shrinks my own team.
I'd likely keep a job, but the **four people** under me might not.
do: **Ask for a role** as claims systems lead with a pay rise.
Take a **cheap online course** in data and automation.
**Bring the team** into a union for proper terms.
feel: **Excited and guilty** at once, because the tools she loves cost friends jobs.
S1.quote: Building the tool and fighting for my team are the same job to me.
fieldNote: She feels **personally responsible** for job cuts her prompts may cause.
She uses her inside knowledge as **leverage** for keeping humans on hard calls.
Her own pay could shrink if Fernhill fails, so **anxious** fits.

steps.text: Ask Fernhill for a claims systems lead role with a pay rise
Take a cheap evening course in data and automation
Sign the claims team up to a finance workers' union
Write down how her AI prompts and checks work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income and fast, because there isn't time for anything else. I'd be online a lot, probably too much, sharing ideas for how the gains could be shared. At work I'd say what I really think, which is that Fernhill won't need a claims desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 AGI does my entire job, including the clever bits I'm proud of. Robots for hands-on work come three years later, but I don't have a hands-on job to hide in. Being good with the tools only matters if there's still a human job next to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year trying to get into the companies building or checking these systems, because someone has to test them. I'd apply for remote jobs testing AI claim decisions, even badly paid ones. Robin's bus job might last until the robots arrive in 2031, so we'd lean on that and cut everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit dizzy. My whole plan was to be the person who knows the tools. In two years that stops being worth anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Robin cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, which we barely use anyway, and the streaming apps. Then we'd look at a cheaper flat, maybe away from the sea. Robin would hate leaving, because Robin's mum lives five minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI every day in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, I'd be using it to find work, write applications, all of it. That's the strange bit. The same thing that takes my job would help me look for the next one.

say: I'd call for a **basic income**, fast, because there's no time for anything else.
I'd say openly that Fernhill **won't need** a claims desk.
think: AGI does my **entire job** by 2028, including the clever parts.
I have **no hands-on work** to shelter in during the three-year robot gap.
do: **Apply for remote jobs** testing AI claim decisions.
**Sell the car** and cancel the streaming apps.
**Lean on Robin's** bus wage until about 2031.
feel: **Scared and dizzy**, as her plan to be the tool expert stops working.
S2.quote: Being good with the tools only matters if there's still a human job next to them.
fieldNote: Her adaptive edge **disappears** when AI does the whole job.
She knows her partner's **hands-on job** buys the household a few years.
She expects to **lose her job** and income, which is alarmed, though she has some plans.

steps.text: Apply for remote jobs testing AI claim decisions
Sell the car and cancel the streaming apps
Live mainly on Robin's bus wage until about 2031
Campaign online for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if we're honest now. I'd push for rules that make insurers keep a human on refused claims and complaints. I'd probably start a small newsletter about AI in insurance, which I've wanted to do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could use those five years to move from claims into checking AI systems for fairness. Insurers will need people who can show regulators the AI isn't refusing claims unfairly. That's a thinking job too, but it's the last thinking job to go, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time certificate in data ethics or audit in the first year, and pay it monthly. I'd volunteer to be Fernhill's contact for the regulator, so I learn that side. And I'd start saving properly, even a hundred a month, once the credit card is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but focused. It feels like a race I could win. I wouldn't sleep perfectly, but I'd have something to do with the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the last thinking job to go. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely, if I'm honest. AGI that can do almost any thinking work could probably audit itself. I'm betting regulators will still want a person to blame, which is a strange thing to build a career on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving away from the coast for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, around year three, if the audit jobs are all in the city. Robin would find that hard, because of family nearby. We'd have that talk properly, not in a hurry.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to get ahead of AGI if we're honest now.
I'd push for rules that keep a **human** on refused claims and complaints.
think: I could move from claims into **checking AI** for fairness.
I'm betting regulators will still want **a person to blame**.
do: **Start a certificate** in data ethics or audit, paid monthly.
**Volunteer** as Fernhill's contact for the regulator.
**Save £100 a month** once the credit card is clear.
feel: **Nervous but focused**, like a race she could win.
S3.quote: I'm betting regulators will still want a person to blame, which is a strange thing to build a career on.
fieldNote: She sees **fairness auditing** as a bridge job and admits it may not last.
A possible **move to the city** would strain her partner's family ties.
Her income could still shrink, but she feels **in control**, so anxious fits.

steps.text: Start a part-time certificate in data ethics or audit
Volunteer as Fernhill's contact for the insurance regulator
Save £100 a month after clearing the credit card
Talk with Robin about moving to the city around year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and we'd be foolish to waste it. I'd want the government to set up paid retraining now and tie it to firms that cut staff. I'd tell the team at Fernhill that we have time, but not to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine in ten years, maybe better than fine. I'd have time to finish an audit qualification, get experience, and move into a job checking AI before AGI lands. What worries me is everyone around me who doesn't like this stuff the way I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Fernhill for two or three years and build the tools properly, with my name on them. I'd do the audit qualification slowly, and pay off every debt before 2030. I'd also help start a union branch, so the people who aren't like me get a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a knot in my stomach for my friends. My own path looks clear. The town's doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. Is anything about your own life not fine in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, still. A decade doesn't fix two weeks of savings and a damp flat. But it gives me time to fix them myself, which is all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum at work, and my partner Robin, honestly. The buses get robots around 2039, and Robin will be in their forties. I'd want Robin thinking about it by 2030, not 2038.

say: I'd call a decade **a gift** we'd be foolish to waste.
I'd want **paid retraining** now, tied to firms that cut staff.
think: I'd have time to finish an **audit qualification** and move before AGI lands.
My worry is **everyone around me** who doesn't enjoy this stuff like I do.
do: **Build the tools** at Fernhill properly for two or three years.
Help **start a union branch** at Fernhill.
feel: **Hopeful** for herself, with a **knot** in her stomach for friends.
S4.quote: A decade doesn't fix two weeks of savings and a damp flat.
fieldNote: She expects her **own path** to hold, so uneasy rather than anxious.
Her concern shifts to **colleagues** and her partner's later robot risk.
Even here, **thin money** stays on her mind.

steps.text: Build Fernhill's AI claims tools with her name on them
Take an audit qualification slowly over several years
Help start a union branch at Fernhill

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because being good with the tools stops mattering overnight. What would help is a basic income or something like it, and rules that make insurers keep people on refused claims. I'd also want cheap training that you can do while working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how it feels to be the one building it. People think the tech-friendly ones are fine. Some days I think I'm automating my friends out of work, and nobody asks me about that.

headlineQuote: Some days I think I'm automating my friends out of work, and nobody asks me about that.
portrait: Maya, 27, runs the claims desk at a **small pet insurer** and uses AI tools daily.
She and her partner Robin rent a damp flat with **two weeks** of savings and a credit card debt.
She is **progressive** and wants a union, even while building the tools that shrink her team.
She is uneasy in AI Plateau and **alarmed** by AGI in 2028, when her tool skills stop counting.
With ten years, she plans a move into **AI auditing** and feels hopeful for herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her skill with the tools would stop mattering overnight.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and rules keeping people on refused claims.
**Cheap training** that she can do while still working.
